big_idea: The single greatest lever for growth and leadership effectiveness is asking good questions, of yourself, your team, and mentors, because, as Maxwell puts it, you only get answers to the questions you actually ask.

tool.label: The Five Whys
tool.text: A questioning technique where a leader keeps asking why in response to each answer, roughly five times in a row, to move from a surface-level symptom to the underlying reasoning or motivation behind a problem or decision. Maxwell applies it both to diagnosing team or process problems and to leaders examining their own motives and blind spots.
tool.note: The Five Whys technique predates this book, it originated in Toyota's production system; Maxwell adapts it for leadership self-examination and team problem-solving rather than originating it.

ideas.title: Questions as Self-Education
ideas.text: You only get answers to the questions you ask, so the quality of a leader's questions caps the quality of their own growth.

ideas.title: Overcoming the Fear of Asking
ideas.text: Leaders often avoid questions to appear competent, but asking demonstrates humility and confidence rather than weakness.

ideas.title: Self-Directed Questions
ideas.text: Leaders need to honestly interrogate their own blind spots, ego, and motives before they can credibly lead others.

ideas.title: Spotting Future Leaders
ideas.text: Maxwell frames traits like initiative, influence on peers, and follow-through as questions to ask when evaluating who's ready for more responsibility.

ideas.title: Question Brainstorming Groups
ideas.text: Regularly scheduled sessions where a team poses open questions about shared challenges instead of pushing pre-formed answers.

ideas.title: A Listening Journal
ideas.text: A habit of recording key insights and follow-up questions after significant conversations, to close the loop on what you're learning from others.

try_it: In your next one-on-one, ask one open why or what question and let the silence sit instead of filling it with your own answer.
Start a listening journal this week: after each significant conversation, jot down one insight and one follow-up question.
Pick one recurring team problem and run the Five Whys on it in your next team meeting.
Ask a trusted peer one question about your own blind spots or leadership weaknesses, and just listen to the answer without defending yourself.
best_for: Leaders who default to giving answers or directives rather than asking
Anyone preparing to do more mentoring, coaching, or one-on-one conversations
less_useful: Readers looking for one overarching leadership theory rather than a question-by-question, almost FAQ-style structure
May feel repetitive alongside Maxwell's other list- or Q&A-style books

related.why: A complementary framework for the feedback conversations these questions often lead into
The same author's broader framework for developing leadership influence
